content.intro: This lesson focuses on json across programming languages and connects the PDF syllabus topics to a small, inspectable example. Work from the intended data model, write down the expected result, then verify syntax and semantics with the target tool.
content.why_it_matters: JSON Across Programming Languages matters because structured-data files sit between people, tools, services, and deployment systems. A clear contract and repeatable checks make the result easier to maintain and safer to consume.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: JSON is a common representation for HTTP payloads and application boundaries. Reliable APIs define stable resource shapes, validate input, report errors consistently, version contracts carefully, and avoid confusing transport status with payload content.

content_blocks.title: What you will cover
content_blocks.text: This lesson explicitly addresses: Language-specific parsing APIs. Language-specific serialization APIs. Mapping objects, dictionaries, maps, and arrays.; Numeric representation differences. Date conversion conventions. Missing values and null mapping. Cross-language compatibility tests.. Treat each as part of a workflow: define what the data should mean, represent it consistently, and test how the chosen implementation interprets it.

content_blocks.title: Inspectable example: JSON Across Programming Languages
content_blocks.code:
JSON number 3  → Python int / JavaScript Number (precision limits differ)
JSON null      → Python None / JavaScript null
JSON array     → Python list / JavaScript Array
JSON object    → Python dict / JavaScript object
content_blocks.expected_output: Mappings between JSON values and runtime types vary by language; test large integers, missing members, dates, and null behavior across consumers.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating readable text as proof of correctness.
common_mistakes.why: Syntax and visual formatting cannot establish data types, schema conformance, or application-specific meaning.
common_mistakes.fix: Parse, validate against the intended contract, and test a valid plus an invalid fixture.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming every parser interprets the feature identically.
common_mistakes.why: Format versions, schema choices, library defaults, and product-specific restrictions affect behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: Record the exact parser/version and test the target environment.

common_mistakes.why: Missing fields, wrong types, duplicate keys, or ambiguous scalars may still break consumers.
common_mistakes.fix: Keep valid, invalid, and boundary fixtures in version control.
